chom

A South African ride app that treats driving like a job

Local platform, local ownership10% commission, half saved for the driverThree asks, one per department
Proof of concept · Department of Transport · Department of Communications and Digital Technologies · Job-creation priority offices
1
Slide 1 · 1.0 min

Good morning, and thank you for making time to see me. My name is Aurelie Msiza, and I am here to show you Chom, a ride-hailing platform built in South Africa for South African conditions. In one sentence: Chom takes the same kind of commission riders already accept, and puts half of it into a savings account in the driver's name. Around that, it adds safety checks that make sure the person driving is the person the app says. I will finish with one specific request for each of your departments. In the middle, I will show you the working app, both the rider side and the driver side, running live.

Where we are

E-hailing is now part of how South African cities move

🚌
Daily transport
To work, the clinic and home after dark, where buses and taxis don't reach
👷
A livelihood
For many drivers, their main or only income
🌍
Offshore
Largest operators headquartered abroad
2
Slide 2 · 1.5 min

E-hailing is no longer a convenience for a few people in Sandton. For many South Africans it is how they get to work, to the clinic, and home at night, especially where public transport is thin or does not run late. It fills gaps that buses, trains and minibus taxis do not cover, particularly after dark and outside the main routes. On the other side of each trip is a driver. For a large number of them, this is their main income, or their only income. Many of them rent the car they drive, so a bad week can mean they owe money rather than earn it. The platforms that carry most of these trips are headquartered outside South Africa. That matters for two reasons I will come back to. Pricing rules are set elsewhere and applied here. And a share of every fare, along with the technology and the data, sits offshore. None of this is a criticism of the people who built those platforms. It is a description of where we are, and it is the starting point for what Chom does differently.

The problem

The current model leaves both riders and drivers exposed

Riders
  • Is the driver who the app says?
  • Surge pricing when you need a ride most
Drivers
  • No cushion, no sick pay
  • Fuel rises faster than fares
3
Slide 3 · 2.0 min

Let me take riders first. When you get into an e-hailing car today, you have limited assurance that the person driving is the person on the profile. Accounts get shared, lent or rented out, and the rider has no way to tell. The second problem for riders is price. During a demand surge, the same trip can cost two or three times as much, and the rider only finds out at the moment they need the ride most. For drivers the problems are different and, I think, harder. A driver on an e-hailing platform works in a purely informal capacity. There is no savings mechanism, so there is no cushion when the car breaks down or a family emergency hits. There is no paid leave, so a sick day is a day without income. And when the fuel price goes up, the driver pays for it immediately, while fares adjust later, if at all. The result is take-home pay that shrinks quietly from month to month. This creates high turnover. Drivers leave as soon as something better comes along, which is bad for them and bad for riders, because experience on the road is part of safety. So the question I started with was simple. Can a platform charge a normal commission and still give drivers something closer to formal employment?

The model

The 10% commission is split: 5% runs Chom, 5% is saved for the driver

R91.68Driver, paid today (90%)
R5.09Savings
R5.09Chom

One trip from the demo: 10 km, driver 2 km away, fare R101.86

12 months
Savings can be withdrawn
12 days
Paid days off a year, from year two
≈ R17,000
Saved a year, illustrative: about R1,300 in fares a day, 22 days a month
4
Slide 4 · 2.0 min

This is the core of the model. Chom takes a 10% commission on every fare. Five percent pays for running the platform. The other five percent goes into a locked savings account in the driver's name. The driver can withdraw it after twelve months of continuous service on Chom. Once a driver reaches that one-year mark, they also qualify for twelve paid offline days a year. These cover illness or a family emergency, and each day is paid at the driver's own average daily earnings. Here is one real trip from the demo. A ten-kilometre ride, with the driver two kilometres away, costs the rider R101.86. The driver is paid R91.68 the same day. R5.09 goes into their savings, and R5.09 runs the platform. For a driver taking in about R1,300 in fares a day, five days a week, that savings share adds up to roughly R17,000 a year. That figure is an illustration, not a measurement, and the written brief will test it against real driver earnings. Because the savings and the leave are both tied to staying on the platform, the model rewards drivers who stay. That is the employment argument in one line: it turns a short-term gig into a job worth keeping, and it gives the sector a reason to hold on to experienced drivers instead of replacing them.

Road safety

Every trip starts with a verified driver in an inspected car

🙂
Driver face matchAgainst the ID photo, before every trip
🔢
Rider's PIN to startPlus "Is this your car?" colour, make and plate check
🛠
10,000 km or 12 monthsMissed inspection locks the profile automatically
🪪
Licence and PrDPChecked daily. Expired means no trips

Also: silent rider alert · driver panic and hijack mode · route checks · 12-hour fatigue limit

5
Slide 5 · 2.0 min

This slide is for the Department of Transport in particular. Before every trip, the driver scans their face, and the app compares it with the photo on their ID document. If it does not match, the trip cannot start, and our safety team is told. Then the rider gives the driver a four-digit PIN from their own phone. Without it, the trip cannot start either. That stops the other common risk, which is someone getting into a car pretending to be their e-hailing driver. Before getting in, the rider sees the car's colour, make and plate in large print, and is asked a simple question: is this your car? Vehicles must be inspected every 10,000 kilometres or every twelve months, whichever comes first. If a driver misses it, their profile is locked out of new trip requests until the inspection is done. That lock is automatic. It does not depend on someone remembering to check. The same rule applies to the driver's licence and Professional Driving Permit, which we would check against the national system every day. Around these we have built the rest of what you would expect: a silent panic alert for riders, a panic button and a hidden hijack alert for drivers, route checks, and a twelve-hour fatigue limit, after which a driver must rest for six hours.

Pricing

Fares are calculated in the open, from distance and the fuel price

Pickup km+Trip km+Fuel price=Fare
✓ No surge pricing✓ No tipping✓ Breakdown shown before booking
6
Slide 6 · 1.5 min

The fare is calculated from three things: how far the driver has to travel to reach the rider, how far the trip is, and the current official fuel price. Every rider can open a breakdown before they book and see each line, including the fuel price we used. There is no surge pricing. The same trip costs the same at five in the afternoon as at three in the morning. There is also no tipping in the app. That is deliberate. Tipping can hide a wage that is too low, and we would rather the fare pay the driver properly. Because the fuel price is part of the formula, when petrol goes up, fares adjust with it, and the driver is not the one absorbing the increase. Including the pickup distance matters too. Today a driver often drives several kilometres to reach a rider and is not paid for it. On Chom, that distance is part of the fare.

7
Slide 7 · 6.0 min

What you are looking at is the working proof of concept. The rider app is on the left and the driver app is on the right, and they are talking to each other live. Let me start as a rider. I am in Sandton, and I want to go to Rosebank. I type the destination, and the app suggests places as I type. I could also drop a pin on the map or use my current location. The app shows the distance, the time and the price. Next to the price is a button that says fare breakdown. Here you can see exactly what I am paying for. This is the driver's distance to me, this is the trip distance, and this is the fuel price we used. At the bottom it shows where the money goes: ninety percent to the driver today, five percent to the driver's savings, five percent to Chom.

The panel on the right is a presenter panel. It lets me change things that would take weeks to happen in real life, like the fuel price, or how long a driver has been on Chom. If I raise the official fuel price by one rand a litre, every fare in the rider app updates straight away, and the breakdown shows the new price. That is how a fuel increase reaches the fare automatically, instead of coming out of the driver's pocket. I will put it back. I can also split this fare with friends from my contacts, schedule it for later, book it for someone else, or ask for a woman driver. I will request it now.

On the driver's phone, a request arrives. Look at what the driver sees first. It is how much they will earn, with Chom's ten percent already taken off, and the part that goes into their own savings. They see where the rider is and where they are going, and they can accept or decline. If they only want trips heading home, they can switch on a filter for that. I will accept. The driver drives to the pickup, and the rider can watch the car approaching.

Now the driver has arrived. On the rider's phone, it says your driver has arrived, and it asks: is this your car? It shows the colour, the make and the plate in large print. I confirm. The driver cannot start the trip yet. First they scan their face. The app is comparing it with the ID on file. That has passed, and the rider's phone now shows face verified. Next, the driver needs the rider's PIN. The rider reads it out, and the driver types it in. Only now can the driver press start trip. During the trip, the rider has a safety bar: a masked call, a message, an audio recording, and a silent alert they can hold down without the driver seeing anything.

Now the trip is complete. The rider sees the receipt. There is no tip button. Instead, it tells the rider how much the driver earned today and how much went into their savings. On the driver's side, the trip summary shows the fare, Chom's five percent, the five percent saved, and what they were paid. Let me open the driver's wallet. This driver has been on Chom for fourteen months, so they can already withdraw their savings. Below that are the paid offline days: twelve a year, paid at their average daily earnings. If I move this driver back to four months on Chom, you can see the savings lock again, with the date they become available.

One last thing. I will make this driver's inspection overdue. Straight away the driver is taken offline, the profile is locked, and the go button cannot be pressed until the inspection is booked and passed. That is the rule working on its own, without anyone having to enforce it by hand. Everything you have just seen runs in a browser today. A production version would connect to real payments, real identity verification and the national traffic systems, which is part of what I would like to discuss with you.

Coverage

Built for all of South Africa, not only city centres

🏘
Township and rural pickupsRider pays at most 2 km of pickup. Chom pays the driver the rest, plus a bonus
📍
Landmark pickups"Blue gate next to the spaza." No street address needed
🗣
Five languagesEnglish, isiZulu, isiXhosa, Afrikaans, Sesotho, with spoken driver prompts
♿
Chom AssistWheelchair-accessible cars at the standard price

ETAs adjust for load-shedding, because trips take longer when traffic lights are out

8
Slide 8 · 2.0 min

Many South Africans live in places that ride apps serve badly. In a township or a rural town, the nearest driver may be far away, and drivers are reluctant to make an unpaid drive to get there. On Chom, a rider in those areas pays for no more than two kilometres of the driver's drive to them. Chom pays the driver the rest, plus a coverage bonus. So a driver is never out of pocket for serving Soweto or Diepsloot instead of Sandton. Many homes there also have no street address that a map recognises. People give directions by landmarks: the blue gate next to the spaza, opposite the taxi rank. Chom lets riders describe their pickup that way, and the driver sees exactly those words. The app runs in English, isiZulu, isiXhosa, Afrikaans and Sesotho, and the driver hears trip prompts spoken in their language, which matters when your eyes should be on the road. Before launch, every translation will be reviewed by native speakers. There is a wheelchair-accessible category, priced exactly the same as the standard ride, because accessibility should not cost the rider more. And estimated times take load-shedding into account, because when traffic lights are out, trips take longer. A platform designed elsewhere would not think to build that.

Digital sovereignty

A South African platform keeps the value, the data and the jobs here

🇿🇦
Value stays in SACommission, data and IP held here, under POPIA
💻
Local tech jobsEngineering, operations and support
⛽
Local pricingTied to South African fuel prices and rules
🏙
City by cityLaunch in one metro, then expand
9
Slide 9 · 1.5 min

This slide is for the Department of Communications and Digital Technologies. Chom is South African built and South African owned. That means the commission on every fare stays in the local economy, and the trip data and the intellectual property behind the platform are held here, under South African law, including POPIA. It also means local engineering jobs to build, run and support the platform. Those are skilled technology jobs, and they stay in the country as the platform grows. Support teams, inspection partners and driver onboarding would also be based here, close to the drivers they serve. Decisions about pricing and policy are made here, by people who live with the outcomes. A clear example is the fare formula itself. It is tied to South African fuel prices, and it can be adjusted for local rules, rather than being a global template applied the same way in every country. The model is designed to launch in one metro, prove itself, and then expand city by city.

10
Slide 10 · 1.5 min

Let me bring this together department by department. For the Department of Transport, Chom is a road safety measure that enforces itself. Every trip has a verified driver, every car has a current inspection, and every driver has a valid licence and permit, or the app will not give them work. It also respects fatigue limits on its own. For the Department of Communications and Digital Technologies, Chom is a homegrown platform in a sector currently dominated by international companies, with the data, the jobs and the decisions kept in South Africa. And for the job-creation priority, Chom makes e-hailing work look more like formal employment. A driver has savings, a form of paid leave, fair pay for serving underserved areas, and a reason to stay in the sector for years instead of months. Each of those is built into the product, not promised in a policy document. I would like to make one request of each of you.

Here is what I am asking for. From the Department of Transport, I would like guidance on the operating licence route for a pilot in one metro, and a conversation about using the existing vehicle testing network for Chom's inspections. From the Department of Communications and Digital Technologies, I would like an introduction to any programme that supports local digital platforms, and guidance on hosting and data requirements. And from the offices responsible for job creation, I would like a conversation about how Chom's savings and leave model could connect with existing employment and skills programmes. Each of these is a conversation, not a contract. I am not asking for a commitment today. I am asking for the right next conversation with the right people in each of your offices. As a next step, I would like to send you a full written brief within two weeks. It will set out the model, the costs, how the savings and leave would be funded, and a plan for a pilot in one metro. And I would be glad to come back and show the demo to any of your colleagues, in person or online. Thank you. I would welcome your questions, and I would especially like to hear what you think would need to be true for a pilot to go ahead.
